chapters.title: Hash maps & sets
chapters.intro: Trade memory for fast lookup. A set answers whether something has appeared; a map associates a key with a count, index, group, or other state.
clues: Need a complement, duplicate, frequency, or grouping
Repeatedly searching earlier elements
Order is not the main requirement
chapters.avoid: If sorted input lets two pointers solve the task with constant space, consider that. Hashing does not preserve numeric order; use sorting or a TreeMap when ordering matters.
chapters.invariant: Before processing index i, the map summarizes only the prefix [0,i).
chapters.adapt: Choose the key by the equivalence you need: raw value, sorted word, frequency signature, or prefix sum. Store an index for reconstruction, a count for multiplicity, and a boolean/set for existence.
chapters.brute: Try every pair of indices: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space. The repeated work is looking for target-nums[i] in the earlier prefix.
trace: Input [2,7,11,15], target 9; begin with an empty map.
i=1: need 2, found at index 0. Return [0,1].
chapters.edges: Duplicate values such as [3,3], target 6; do not reuse the same index; clarify whether an answer is guaranteed; expected hash cost is not an unconditional worst-case guarantee.

chapters.title: Two pointers
chapters.intro: Coordinate two positions so each movement either eliminates impossible candidates or maintains a useful processed region. Opposite-end pointers exploit order; read/write pointers compact data in place.
clues: Sorted array and a pair target
In-place filtering or stable compaction
A proof lets one endpoint be discarded
chapters.avoid: Do not move pointers just because a sum is too small unless ordering supports that elimination. For arbitrary unsorted pair lookup, a hash map is usually simpler.
chapters.invariant: Any possible pair remains inside the current candidate interval; for read/write scans, the written prefix contains exactly the accepted processed values.
chapters.adapt: For 3Sum, fix one index then solve the remaining pair. For stable filtering, replace opposite ends with read/write indices. Handle duplicates based on whether answers are indices or unique values.
chapters.brute: Check all pairs, O(n²). Sorting already supplied by Two Sum II lets one comparison remove an entire row of candidate pairs.
chapters.edges: Two-element input; duplicates; correct 0-based versus 1-based result; long arithmetic for sums.

chapters.title: Sliding window
chapters.intro: Maintain a contiguous range and update its state as boundaries move. Fixed windows keep a chosen width; variable windows expand and shrink according to a validity condition.
clues: Substring or contiguous subarray
Longest/shortest range meeting a condition
Can update range state on add/remove and safely discard left endpoints
chapters.avoid: Contiguous alone is insufficient. With negative numbers, sum-based expand/shrink rules often fail: use prefix sums, or prefix sums plus a monotonic deque for shortest sum-at-least-K.
chapters.invariant: For longest-valid-window scans, the window is valid before its length is recorded.
chapters.adapt: For shortest-valid windows, record the length WHILE valid, then shrink. For fixed width, remove the element falling out and evaluate only full windows. Keep counts synchronized with boundary changes.
chapters.brute: Enumerate all substrings and check uniqueness from scratch: O(n³). Incremental sets per start improve to O(n²); a shared moving window avoids rescanning starts.
trace: right=2 adds b twice: remove a, then the old b; left=2, window "b".
right=3 adds a; window "ba", best stays 2.
chapters.edges: Empty string; all same characters; a duplicate before the current left boundary; positive-values assumption for sum windows; fixed-size window larger than input.

chapters.title: Prefix sums & prefix/suffix accumulation
chapters.intro: Summarize each prefix once. Subtract two prefix sums for a range total; match earlier prefix sums to count target-sum ranges. Prefix/suffix products extend the idea to a non-subtractive operation.
clues: Many static range queries
Count subarrays with an exact sum, including negatives
Combine everything before and after an index
chapters.avoid: Prefix sums do not directly give range minima by subtraction. Frequent updates call for different data structures; product variants need separate reasoning around zeros.
chapters.invariant: prefix[i] summarizes the first i elements. When counting ranges, the frequency map contains only earlier prefix boundaries.
chapters.adapt: Use counts for number of ranges, earliest indices for longest ranges, and a set for existence. For product-except-self, store left products and sweep backward with a right product.
chapters.brute: Try every start and extend its sum to every end: O(n²) time. A range sum equals currentPrefix-earlierPrefix, so exact-sum counting becomes a lookup.
trace: Second 1: sum=2, need 0 occurs once; answer=1; record 2.
Third 1: sum=3, need 1 occurs once; answer=2.
chapters.edges: Seed empty prefix; query before insert; zeros create multiple valid starts; negative numbers are supported; sums can overflow int.

chapters.title: Sort, then scan
chapters.intro: Sorting creates structure that makes local comparisons sufficient. Often an unordered global problem becomes a one-pass scan over neighboring candidates.
clues: Group equivalent objects
Merge or schedule ranges
A custom ordering makes a greedy/local decision provable
chapters.avoid: Sorting changes input order and costs more than a linear scan. Preserve original indices when needed. A comparator must be consistent; do not invent an ordering without a correctness argument.
chapters.invariant: The processed sorted prefix has a finalized answer except for the current open group.
chapters.adapt: Sort by start for merging, by end for interval scheduling, and by a canonical signature for grouping. Largest Number uses concatenation order, not ordinary numeric order.
chapters.brute: Repeatedly compare and merge overlapping pairs until stable; naive implementations do unnecessary repeated scans. Sorting starts gives a direct O(n log n) solution.
trace: Keep [1,3]; next start 2 <= 3, extend end to 6.
chapters.edges: Empty input when permitted; equal keys; comparator overflow from a-b; whether sorting the original array is allowed.

chapters.title: Binary search: exact & boundary
chapters.intro: Repeatedly discard half of an ordered candidate space. Decide first whether you need an exact match or the first position satisfying a predicate; their loop contracts differ.
clues: Sorted values
Find first/last occurrence or insertion position
One half can be proved irrelevant
chapters.avoid: Sorted-looking data is not enough: establish a monotone predicate or a safe elimination argument. Rotated-array search needs its own sorted-half logic.
chapters.invariant: Exact closed search keeps any target inside [left,right]. Half-open lower bound keeps the first true boundary between left and right, allowing n.
chapters.adapt: Use > instead of >= for upper bound. An exact closed search uses right=n-1 and left<=right, with mid±1 updates. Never mix interval conventions midway.
chapters.brute: Linear search is O(n). An ascending array tells us that every element on one side of mid is also too small or too large.
trace: If a target is absent, the closed interval eventually becomes empty.
chapters.edges: Empty array; one element; absent target; duplicates; answer can be n for boundary search; prevent midpoint overflow.

chapters.title: Binary search on the answer
chapters.intro: Turn an optimization task into a monotone yes/no feasibility test. Search possible answers rather than positions in the input.
clues: Minimize a maximum or find the smallest sufficient capacity/speed
Checking a proposed answer is easier than constructing the optimum
If x works, every larger x works (or the reverse)
chapters.avoid: First prove monotonicity and the feasibility routine. A flawed greedy checker makes the entire search wrong even when the binary-search loop is correct.
chapters.invariant: The minimum feasible answer lies in [low,high], and high is feasible.
chapters.adapt: Choose tight legal bounds. Multiply number of feasibility checks by their cost. For a largest-feasible search, change the update convention and midpoint carefully rather than copying this loop unchanged.
chapters.brute: Try each speed from 1 to M and scan piles: O(nM). Feasibility can change only from false to true, allowing logarithmically many scans.
trace: Piles [3,6,7,11], h=8, bounds [1,11]. speed 6 needs 6 hours → high=6.
chapters.edges: Infeasible inputs if the task permits them; all-zero domains in variants; ceil division; long totals; exactly-k versus at-most-k groups.

chapters.title: Interval merging & overlap
chapters.intro: Represent spans by endpoints and reason about where one starts relative to another’s end. Merging, insertion, and selecting non-overlapping spans share inputs but require different objectives.
clues: Ranges, meetings, reservations, spans
Merge coverage or insert a range
Count removals to make ranges compatible
chapters.avoid: Do not treat merging coverage as interval scheduling. Merging usually sorts by start; selecting the most compatible intervals usually sorts by end.
chapters.invariant: For merging, completed result intervals are disjoint and sorted, and the last one captures all overlap seen so far.
chapters.adapt: Decide closed versus half-open endpoints before writing <= or <. Insert Interval can avoid sorting because its input is already sorted and disjoint.
chapters.brute: Checking each interval against every other gives quadratic pair comparisons and still requires organizing transitive merges. Sorting exposes overlaps in a single forward scan.
trace: Current [1,3], next [2,6]: overlap because 2<=3; merged becomes [1,6].
chapters.edges: Nested intervals; touching boundaries; duplicate intervals; negative endpoints; do not overwrite end without taking max.

chapters.title: Sweep line & difference events
chapters.intro: Process only positions where something changes. Record signed changes at boundaries, order them, and accumulate active load or coverage.
clues: Maximum simultaneous activity
Capacity over time or distance
Many range additions with one final reconstruction
chapters.avoid: Endpoint semantics determine event ordering. For real-valued closed intervals, end+1 is not valid; explicitly process start/end ties. Difference arrays work best on bounded integer coordinates.
chapters.invariant: After combining events at coordinate x, the running total equals the load on the segment immediately after x under the chosen endpoint convention.
chapters.adapt: For closed integer ranges, subtract at end+1 using a wide coordinate type. For a small dense coordinate range, an array eliminates sorting/map costs.
chapters.brute: Check every trip against every relevant position or event, potentially O(n²) at O(n) distinct positions. Events summarize each trip using only two updates.
chapters.edges: Pickup and drop-off at the same position; closed endpoints; end+1 overflow; sparse huge coordinates; simultaneous deltas.

chapters.title: Linked-list manipulation
chapters.intro: Reason in terms of node identity and links, not array indices. Dummy nodes simplify head changes; saved next pointers preserve access while relinking.
clues: Reverse or merge nodes in place
Remove a node relative to the head/tail
Head may change as a special case
chapters.avoid: Do not overwrite next before saving the untouched suffix. A linked list has no constant-time indexed access; repeated index-style scans can become quadratic.
chapters.invariant: For reversal, prev heads the reversed prefix and current heads the original unprocessed suffix.
chapters.adapt: Use a dummy before operations that may remove or replace the head. For merging, advance a tail pointer. For nth-from-end, keep a fixed pointer gap rather than a speed ratio.
chapters.brute: Copy values to an array and build a reversed list: O(n) time and O(n) extra allocation. In-place reversal can retain the linear time while reusing nodes.
trace: 1→2→3: prev=null,current=1; save node 2, point 1 to null.
chapters.edges: Empty list; one node; deleting head; losing suffix; creating accidental cycles; whether mutation is allowed.

chapters.title: Fast & slow pointers
chapters.intro: Move two pointers through the same successor relation at different speeds. This reveals midpoints or cycles without storing all visited nodes.
clues: Cycle detection with constant space
Find a midpoint in one traversal
Values define a next-index functional graph
chapters.avoid: Use node identity, not equal values, for cycle detection. Array-as-linked-list tricks require valid index ranges and a specific graph structure.
chapters.invariant: After t iterations, slow has moved t edges and fast 2t; in a cycle their relative position advances modulo its length.
chapters.adapt: For midpoint, return slow after termination. For cycle entry, reset one pointer to the start after meeting, then move both one step until they meet again. A fixed n-node gap is a separate two-pointer variant.
chapters.brute: Store every visited node in a set: expected O(n) time and O(n) memory. Different-speed pointers avoid the visited set.
trace: Second move: slow=node3, fast=node3 → cycle detected.
chapters.edges: Check fast.next before double movement; self-loop; no cycle; compare after moving; even-length midpoint convention.

chapters.title: Stacks: matching & simulation
chapters.intro: Use last-in-first-out order when the most recent unfinished item must be resolved first. Store extra metadata when undoing an operation must restore previous state.
clues: Nested delimiters
Postfix expressions or undo history
Need a value and its historical minimum
chapters.avoid: A queue is for oldest-first processing, such as BFS. A plain stack does not by itself enforce nearest-greater relationships; monotonic stacks add an ordering invariant.
chapters.invariant: The stack represents exactly the unresolved obligations or intermediate results, newest on top.
chapters.adapt: For brackets, store expected closers. For postfix arithmetic, preserve operand order. For Min Stack, store the minimum alongside every pushed value.
chapters.brute: Repeatedly remove adjacent matching pairs until no change: repeated scans/string rebuilding can be O(n²). A stack resolves each bracket once.
trace: Read ) → pop matching ); stack empty → valid.
chapters.edges: Early closer; leftover opener; wrong nesting; empty stack operations; division/subtraction operand order; ArrayDeque rejects null.

chapters.title: Monotonic stack
chapters.intro: Keep unresolved candidates in increasing or decreasing order. A new value resolves and removes candidates that it dominates.
clues: Next greater/smaller element
Nearest boundary satisfying a comparison
Histogram width determined by smaller bars
chapters.avoid: The direction and strictness depend on the task. Equal temperatures are not warmer. Use indices if you need distance or must distinguish duplicates.
chapters.invariant: For Daily Temperatures, stack indices are unresolved and their temperatures are nonincreasing from bottom to top.
chapters.adapt: Reverse comparisons for next smaller; reverse traversal for other directional variants. For histograms, popping fixes a rectangle’s right boundary, while the new top gives its left boundary.
chapters.brute: For each day, scan forward to the first warmer day: O(n²). A stack keeps all unresolved days and settles each once.
trace: 71 cannot resolve 75; push index3. Unresolved answers stay zero.
chapters.edges: Equal values; fully increasing/decreasing arrays; storing values instead of indices when distances are required; sentinel flush for histogram.

chapters.title: Monotonic deque
chapters.intro: Maintain ordered candidates while also expiring candidates from the oldest end. A deque supports both removal reasons efficiently.
clues: Sliding-window maximum or minimum
Need ordered candidates and age-based expiration
Dominated prefixes in shortest-subarray problems
chapters.avoid: A heap can find extrema but may need lazy expiration. A deque works when a dominance proof lets you permanently discard candidates; not every window statistic has one.
chapters.invariant: For window maxima, indices increase front-to-back while their values strictly decrease; every index is still within the window.
chapters.adapt: Use two deques for both max and min. For negative-number shortest sum ranges, use increasing prefix sums and prove separate front/back removal rules.
chapters.brute: Scan each k-element window for its maximum: O(nk). Keeping only undominated unexpired indices avoids those repeated scans.
trace: Insert 3 at index1, discard index0 because it is smaller and older.
Insert -1; first full window max is 3. Insert -3; next max stays 3.
Insert 5: expire index1, discard smaller back candidates; new max is 5.
chapters.edges: k=1; k=n; equal values; expire by index, not value; negative numbers in prefix-deque variants.

chapters.title: Tree DFS & recursive returns
chapters.intro: Define precisely what a recursive call returns for one subtree. Combine child results to answer the parent, and separately track global answers when they cannot be extended upward.
clues: Subtree properties
Height, path, ancestor, or structural comparison
A parent answer can be built from child answers
chapters.avoid: Trees do not need a visited set when traversing child links without cycles. General graphs do. Deep skewed trees can exceed Java’s recursion stack.
chapters.invariant: Each call returns the promised summary for its entire subtree; the null case must be compatible with the combination rule.
chapters.adapt: Height returns one downward branch. Diameter combines two branches for the global answer but returns only height. LCA returns a found target/ancestor, not a numeric depth.
chapters.brute: Enumerate root-to-leaf paths and store them, potentially copying O(nh) data. A height return summarizes each subtree once without retaining paths.
trace: Tree 3 with leaves 9 and subtree 20→(15,7). Null children return 0.
chapters.edges: Null root; one node; skewed tree; edges versus nodes; reset global fields between calls; LCA presence assumptions.

chapters.title: Tree BFS & levels
chapters.intro: Process nodes by increasing depth using a queue. Capture a layer’s size before appending its children so one iteration corresponds to exactly one level.
clues: Level order or per-depth aggregation
Rightmost/leftmost node at each depth
Shortest root-to-leaf distance
chapters.avoid: BFS can use substantial memory on wide trees. DFS may use less memory there but more on deep chains. A null child is not a leaf.
chapters.invariant: At the beginning of each outer iteration, the queue contains exactly the next depth’s nodes in left-to-right order.
chapters.adapt: For right-side view, record the final node in each left-to-right level. For minimum depth, return at the first actual leaf. Do not use a changing queue.size() as the inner-loop bound.
chapters.brute: Repeatedly traverse the tree to collect depth 0, then depth 1, etc.: O(nh) worst case. One queue traversal processes every node once.
chapters.edges: Null root; one-sided trees; broad levels; queue size snapshot; do not enqueue null with ArrayDeque.

chapters.title: BST ordering & inorder
chapters.intro: Exploit the global binary-search-tree property: every value in a left subtree is smaller, and every value in a right subtree larger, under a strict BST convention.
clues: Explicit BST input
Rank queries through sorted inorder traversal
Navigate by comparing target values
chapters.avoid: A binary tree is not automatically a BST. Checking only parent-child values does not validate all descendants. Balanced-tree complexity cannot be assumed.
chapters.invariant: Each recursive node must lie strictly within its inherited (low,high) interval; inorder visits valid BST values in increasing order.
chapters.adapt: For kth smallest, count inorder visits and stop early. For BST LCA, descend only while both target values lie on the same side. Clarify duplicate placement if duplicates are allowed.
chapters.brute: For each node, rescan its left and right subtrees to check all descendants: O(n²) worst case. Inherited bounds capture those constraints once.
trace: Node1 must be in (-∞,5) and is valid.
Node4 must be in (5,+∞), but 4<=5 → reject immediately.
chapters.edges: Integer extreme values; strict versus non-strict ordering; skewed trees; target nodes absent; valid k assumption.

chapters.title: Graph/grid DFS & BFS
chapters.intro: Model states as vertices and legal moves as edges. Traverse connected components with DFS/BFS; use BFS layers for shortest paths when every move has equal cost.
clues: Connectivity, islands, reachability
Fewest equal-cost moves
Several simultaneous spreading sources
chapters.avoid: Ordinary BFS does not solve arbitrary weighted shortest paths. Include all relevant state in visited keys: position alone may be insufficient if keys, remaining eliminations, or other resources matter.
chapters.invariant: A state is marked when discovered so it is scheduled only once; BFS discovery distances are nondecreasing.
chapters.adapt: For components, start a new traversal at each unvisited vertex. For multi-source BFS, enqueue all sources at distance zero. A grid can be marked in place if mutation is allowed.
chapters.brute: Starting an independent flood fill from every land cell without sharing visited information can revisit an island many times. One shared visitation state processes each cell once.
trace: The later scan skips marked cells.
Cell (2,2) starts island2; no adjacent land → total2.
chapters.edges: Disconnected graph; isolated nodes; cycles; four versus eight directions; rectangular bounds; mutation and stack overflow.

chapters.title: Topological sort
chapters.intro: Order a directed acyclic graph so every dependency appears before its dependent. Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with no remaining incoming dependencies.
clues: Prerequisites or task dependency ordering
Can all tasks finish?
Detect a directed cycle through failed dependency elimination
chapters.avoid: Not a general undirected-cycle algorithm. Edge direction matters: prerequisite→dependent. A valid ordering need not be unique.
chapters.invariant: Every queued node has zero incoming edges from unprocessed nodes; every output node appears after all its prerequisites.
chapters.adapt: Record the popped nodes for an ordering. For eventual-safe states, reverse edges and eliminate original terminal nodes. DFS color states provide an alternative directed-cycle test.
chapters.brute: Try every possible task permutation and validate dependencies: factorial work. Incoming-dependency counts identify legal next tasks directly.
trace: Queue starts [0]; process0 and reduce indegree1 to0.
Enqueue/process1; completed=2, so all courses can finish.
Adding edge1→0 leaves no initial zero-indegree node → cycle.
chapters.edges: Isolated vertices; empty prerequisites; disconnected components; duplicate edges counted consistently; return partial ordering only if the task permits it.

chapters.title: Union-find / disjoint sets
chapters.intro: Maintain a partition into connected components as undirected edges are added. Each component has a representative root; union merges roots.
clues: Repeated connectivity queries while adding edges
Count components
Detect whether an undirected edge joins already-connected vertices
chapters.avoid: DSU does not find shortest paths or actual connecting routes. Standard DSU does not support arbitrary deletions or directed-cycle detection.
chapters.invariant: Two vertices have the same representative exactly when processed edges connect them.
chapters.adapt: Use path compression with size/rank balancing. Decrement component count only on a successful union. For sparse labels, map labels to compact indices first.
chapters.brute: Before each edge, run DFS to ask whether its endpoints are connected: O(E(V+E)) over all insertions. DSU retains the evolving connectivity summary.
trace: Edges [1,2],[1,3],[2,3]; initially each vertex is its own root.
For2,3 both finds return the same root → redundant edge [2,3].
chapters.edges: One-based labels; isolated vertices; repeated edges; initialize every node; rank is not component size; failed unions must not change counts.

chapters.title: Dijkstra & best-first paths
chapters.intro: Expand the smallest tentative path cost first. Relax neighbors when a better route is found; with nonnegative edge costs, the smallest unsettled distance is final.
clues: Weighted shortest paths with nonnegative weights
An accumulated path cost is monotone under extension
Bottleneck or probability variants have a compatible best-first proof
chapters.avoid: Negative edges invalidate standard Dijkstra finalization. For equal weights, BFS is simpler. A heap alone does not prove a new path-cost formula is safe.
chapters.invariant: Each nonstale popped state has the best attainable distance to its vertex; stored distances are the best routes discovered so far.
chapters.adapt: Use max(current,edge) for bottleneck effort; use a max-heap and multiplication for probabilities in [0,1]. Store parents if you need to reconstruct a route. Lazy heap duplicates need stale-entry checks.
chapters.brute: Repeatedly relax all edges for up to V-1 passes (Bellman–Ford): O(VE). Nonnegative weights allow a heap to focus work on the next finalized vertex.
trace: Source2; edges2→1(1),2→3(1),3→4(1). Start distances [∞,0,∞,∞] for nodes1..4.
Pop1 and3 at1 in either order; node3 sets dist4=2.
chapters.edges: Unreachable vertices; zero-weight edges; stale entries; directed versus undirected edges; wide distance sums; comparator overflow.

chapters.title: Heaps: Top K, merging & medians
chapters.intro: A heap exposes the best current candidate without fully sorting everything. Keep the weakest retained Top-K item at the root, frontier heads for merging, or two balanced halves for medians.
clues: Top/bottom K rather than a complete sort
Repeated next-best extraction
Sorted streams or online median
chapters.avoid: Heap iteration is not sorted order. PriorityQueue.remove(Object) and contains are linear. Changing a stored object’s priority does not automatically repair the heap.
chapters.invariant: For Top K, the size-k min-heap contains the strongest k candidates processed so far; its root is the weakest retained candidate.
chapters.adapt: Merge K lists: heap one head per list and replace the popped head with its successor. Median: lower max-heap and upper min-heap, ordered and balanced. Define tie-breaking if the output requires it.
chapters.brute: Count frequencies, then sort all u unique values: expected O(n+u log u). A size-k heap reduces selection work when k is small.
trace: Insert1 and2; min-heap root is2 with frequency2.
Insert3, size3; pop3 because it has frequency1.
Retained values are1 and2; output order is irrelevant.
chapters.edges: k=1 or k=unique count; fewer than k values in variants; equal priorities; null list heads; median averaging overflow; empty median query.

chapters.title: Backtracking
chapters.intro: Explore a decision tree while maintaining one mutable partial answer. Choose, recurse, and undo so sibling branches start from the same state.
clues: Generate all subsets, arrangements, or combinations
Small input with exponentially many valid outputs
Constraints permit pruning partial choices
chapters.avoid: For only a count or optimum with overlapping states, DP may avoid enumerating all possibilities. Never claim polynomial time when the output itself is exponential.
chapters.invariant: At function entry, path represents exactly the choices on the current branch; every return restores the caller’s state.
chapters.adapt: Subsets save every path and advance a start index. Permutations use a used array. Reusable combinations recurse from i; one-use combinations from i+1. Duplicate inputs require same-depth duplicate skipping.
chapters.brute: Enumerate every bitmask and copy selected values: O(n2^n). Backtracking has the same unavoidable output order but gives flexible pruning and a reusable decision-tree structure.
trace: Choose1 → save [1]; choose2 → save [1,2]; undo2, undo1.
All four subsets appear once because indices only increase.
chapters.edges: Copy path when saving; undo flags and values; combinations versus permutations; repeated candidates; valid pruning needs a proof (e.g., positivity).

chapters.title: 1D DP & reachable prefixes
chapters.intro: Store answers to overlapping smaller states. Start by defining what one entry means; then derive transitions from a final choice rather than guessing a recurrence.
clues: A sequence of local choices affects future options
Same suffix/prefix state is reached by multiple paths
Count, decide feasibility, or optimize without enumerating every path
chapters.avoid: Greedy is valid only if a local choice can be proved safe. Word Break is a useful counterexample: an early matching word need not belong to a successful segmentation.
chapters.invariant: For Word Break, reachable[i] is true exactly when the first i characters can be fully segmented; reachable[0]=true is the empty-prefix base case.
chapters.adapt: Boolean OR for feasibility, addition for counts, min/max for optimization. Memoization caches recursive states; bottom-up orders their dependencies. Rolling state is safe only if older entries are never needed.
chapters.brute: Recursively try every word boundary with no cache; repeated suffix decisions can cause exponential branching. Cache each prefix/suffix state to avoid recomputing it.
trace: end1,2 stay false; end3 becomes true using [0,3).
end4 becomes true using [0,4); end5 stays false.
end6 uses reachable3 + "aaa"; end7 uses reachable3 + "aaaa" → true.
A greedy aaa+aaa leaves one a, but DP preserves the successful alternative.
chapters.edges: Empty-prefix base case; impossible states; update order; substring copying costs in Java; rolling variables overwritten too early.

chapters.title: Grid DP
chapters.intro: Store the answer for reaching each cell when legal moves form an acyclic dependency structure, commonly right/down movement.
clues: Count or optimize right/down paths
Cell depends only on already-computed neighbors
Obstacles or costs modify a local recurrence
chapters.avoid: If movement can cycle in all directions, simple row-major DP is generally invalid. Use graph traversal or shortest-path methods unless another acyclic order exists.
chapters.invariant: When computing a cell, all of its predecessor states are already final.
chapters.adapt: Use sum for path counts and min+cellCost for minimum cost. Rolling rows retain above in dp[c] and updated left in dp[c-1]. Set obstacle entries to zero, not merely skip them.
chapters.brute: Enumerate all right/down paths: the number grows combinatorially. Many paths reach the same cell; store that cell’s answer once.
trace: Second row: [1,2,3], because each cell adds above and left.
chapters.edges: Single row/column; blocked origin/end; zero paths; boundary initialization; count overflow; accidental input mutation.

chapters.title: Knapsack & coin-change DP
chapters.intro: Index states by a resource total such as sum or capacity. Distinguish using each item once from unlimited reuse, and distinguish counting from minimizing.
clues: Subset reaches a target sum
Capacity or budget bounded by a manageable integer
Minimum coins or number of combinations
chapters.avoid: O(nS) is pseudo-polynomial and may be infeasible when S is huge. Negative item values invalidate simple 0..target indexing. Loop order changes which choices are legal.
chapters.invariant: For 0/1 DP after item i, dp[s] uses only processed items, each at most once.
chapters.adapt: 0/1 items: scan sums down. Unlimited items: scan up. Count unordered combinations: item loop outside. Count ordered sequences: sum loop outside. Minimum coin counts use min and an unreachable sentinel.
chapters.brute: Try all 2^n subsets. Different subsets often reach the same sum at the same item stage, so DP merges those equivalent states.
trace: [1,5,11,5] totals22; target11; initially only sum0 reachable.
chapters.edges: Odd total; target zero; sentinel arithmetic; downward versus upward scan; duplicate denominations; counting order.

chapters.title: Sequence & two-string DP
chapters.intro: For two sequences, track a pair of prefix lengths. For a single subsequence, an endpoint state often captures which earlier choices can extend into the current element.
clues: Subsequence rather than substring
Compare or transform two strings
Choose/skip characters while preserving order
chapters.avoid: Subsequences need not be contiguous. Longest common substring uses a different recurrence. An LIS tails array gives length but is not necessarily an actual subsequence.
chapters.invariant: LCS dp[i][j] is the best shared subsequence length of a[0:i] and b[0:j]. Empty-prefix answers are zero.
chapters.adapt: Edit distance minimizes insert/delete/replace costs. LIS endpoint DP compares all earlier smaller values; the O(n log n) extension keeps minimal tails and uses lower bound. Retain parent/choice data to reconstruct a sequence.
chapters.brute: Enumerate subsequences of one string and test them against the other: exponential work. Prefix pairs repeat, so an m×n table replaces branching with shared states.
trace: a="abc", b="ac"; start with a zero row/column.
After b: row [0,1,1], since b matches neither character.
After c: row [0,1,2] using diagonal+1 at c/c; answer2.
chapters.edges: Empty strings; repeated letters; strict versus non-strict LIS; prefix lengths versus character indices; reconstructing versus only computing length.

chapters.title: Greedy
chapters.intro: Make a local choice that can be proved safe, or maintain a compressed summary sufficient for all future choices. The proof is the method, not an afterthought.
clues: An exchange argument preserves an optimum
A farther-reaching state dominates weaker states
Sorting exposes a safe first choice
chapters.avoid: Do not assume local improvement implies global optimality. Coin denominations [1,3,4] with amount6 defeat largest-coin-first; Word Break defeats first-match-first.
chapters.invariant: For Jump Game, every index up to farthest is reachable from the processed reachable prefix.
chapters.adapt: Interval scheduling chooses earliest finish and uses an exchange proof. Stock profit retains the minimum earlier price. Explain why discarded alternatives can never improve the answer.
chapters.brute: Try every possible jump sequence: exponential in the worst case. A DP can track reachable indices in O(n²); the contiguous reachable frontier compresses it to one value.
trace: Last index is now covered → true.
For [3,2,1,0,4], frontier stalls at3; index4 is unreachable.
chapters.edges: Zero jumps; first/last index; one element; unsupported greedy choices; maintaining coverage is not the same as jumping to the largest immediate value.

chapters.title: Tries & prefix search
chapters.intro: Store words as shared character paths. This makes prefix existence and prefix-guided branching explicit instead of comparing every stored word.
clues: Many prefix queries
Dictionary wildcard matching
Shortest root prefix or prefix-pruned word search
chapters.avoid: For exact membership alone, a hash set may be simpler and more compact. Fixed 26-child arrays assume lowercase English and spend memory on empty child slots.
chapters.invariant: The node after consuming a prefix represents exactly that prefix; terminal state distinguishes a stored word from a partial path.
chapters.adapt: For dot wildcards, DFS into each child. For root replacement, stop at the first terminal. Use a map of children for broader alphabets. Combine trie + backtracking for multiword board search.
chapters.brute: Store a list of words and scan each for every prefix query: O(D·L) in a simple worst-case model with D words and query length L. A trie follows a single prefix path.
trace: Insert "apple": create/follow a→p→p→l→e; mark only e terminal.
search("app") follows a→p→p but terminal=false → false.
Insert "app" marks that p terminal; exact search now succeeds.
chapters.edges: Prefix versus complete word; repeated insertions; alphabet constraints; empty string policy; wildcard explosion; fixed child-array memory.

chapters.title: Bit manipulation
chapters.intro: Use fixed-width binary representation directly. XOR cancels paired values, masks isolate flags, and shifts relate neighboring binary states.
clues: Every value repeats except one
Subset/flag representation
Count or test set bits with constant-width arithmetic
chapters.avoid: XOR cancellation depends on the exact repetition pattern. Twice-except-one differs from three-times-except-one. Java signed shifts and overflow need explicit reasoning.
chapters.invariant: The running XOR equals the XOR of the processed prefix; paired values cancel regardless of order.
chapters.adapt: Use 1L<<bit for long masks. >>> is zero-fill right shift; >> preserves the sign bit. Java masks shift distances (int: mod32, long: mod64), so validate the bit range.
chapters.brute: Count values in a map: expected O(n) time and O(n) space. XOR uses the promised pair structure to eliminate that memory.
chapters.edges: Negative ints; zero; bit31; shift width; operator precedence; distinguish O(number of bits) from O(1) at fixed machine width.

1.title: Two Sum
1.prompt: Return indices of two different elements whose sum equals target. Exactly one answer exists.
hints: For each number, what other number would complete the pair?
Store earlier values and their indices; look up the complement before inserting the current value.
1.approach: A map remembers exactly the processed prefix. Checking before insertion prevents reusing the same index.
1.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Each element makes a constant number of expected-constant-time hash operations.

49.title: Group Anagrams
49.prompt: Group strings that contain the same letters with the same multiplicities. Inputs contain lowercase English letters.
hints: What representation stays the same when letters are rearranged?
Sort the characters of each word and use that string as a map key.
49.approach: Words have equal sorted keys exactly when they are anagrams. Append each original word to its key’s group.
49.cost: O(n k log k) time for n words of maximum length k; O(nk) space for keys and grouped references (including returned grouping). Hashing a length-k key also costs O(k).

128.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
128.prompt: Find the length of the longest consecutive-value sequence in an unsorted array, in O(n) expected time.
hints: A sequence only needs to be counted from its smallest value.
Put values in a set; start a forward walk only when x-1 is absent.
128.approach: Each distinct value is traversed in only one sequence. Duplicates disappear in the set.
128.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space. The nested walk visits each distinct value once across all sequence starts.

167.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
167.prompt: In a nondecreasing array, find two distinct values totaling target; return their 1-based indices.
hints: How does sorting constrain which movement can improve a sum that is too small?
Start at both ends. Increase left for a small sum; decrease right for a large sum.
167.approach: If the sum is too small, the current left value cannot pair with any remaining right value. The symmetric argument eliminates right when the sum is too large.
167.cost: O(n) time because each pointer moves at most n times; O(1) auxiliary space.

15.title: 3Sum
15.prompt: Return unique triplets of values summing to zero.
hints: Fix one value; what familiar problem remains?
Sort, then use two pointers for the remaining pair. Skip duplicate fixed and paired values.
15.approach: Sorting makes duplicate elimination and directional pair search possible. This solution changes the input order.
15.cost: O(n²) time. O(log n) typical sorting stack space, excluding O(z) output for z triplets; scan uses O(1) extra space.

283.title: Move Zeroes
283.prompt: Move all zeros to the end in place, preserving the order of nonzero values.
hints: Track where the next retained value belongs.
Copy each nonzero to a write pointer, then fill the remaining suffix with zeros.
283.approach: The prefix before write always contains the encountered nonzero values in their original order.
283.cost: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; each position is read once and written at most a constant number of times.

3.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
3.prompt: Return the longest length of a contiguous substring with no repeated characters.
hints: Maintain one contiguous range rather than restarting for every left endpoint.
Count characters in a window; after adding the right character, remove from the left until its count is one.
3.approach: Before recording a length, all window characters are distinct. Every longer range ending at right was invalid.
3.cost: Expected O(n) time; O(min(n, alphabet size)) space. Each UTF-16 char is added once and removed at most once. This implementation counts Java char units, not arbitrary Unicode grapheme clusters.

209.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
209.prompt: For positive integers and a positive target, return the shortest nonempty subarray with sum at least target, or 0.
hints: Positivity means extending never decreases the sum.
Expand right, then repeatedly shrink while the sum is large enough, recording lengths before removal.
209.approach: Shrinking enumerates the valid left boundaries needed for the shortest window at each right boundary.
209.cost: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Both endpoints move only forward. Negative numbers would invalidate the shrink rule.

567.title: Permutation in String
567.prompt: For lowercase strings, determine whether s2 contains a substring that is a permutation of s1.
hints: A permutation has the same length and letter frequencies.
Slide a window of length s1.length(), compare two arrays of 26 counts.
567.approach: Once the window has the target length, equality of all counts is necessary and sufficient.
567.cost: O(m + 26n) = O(m+n) time for lengths m,n; O(26) = O(1) extra space under the lowercase-English constraint.

560.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
560.prompt: Count nonempty contiguous subarrays summing to k; values may be negative.
hints: A range sum is the difference between two prefix sums.
At prefix sum s, count earlier prefixes equal to s-k. Seed frequency 0 with 1.
560.approach: Earlier prefix occurrences represent distinct starting positions. Query before adding the current prefix to avoid counting an empty range.
560.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space. The answer uses int under the problem’s size limits; larger inputs may need a long count.

303.title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
303.prompt: Preprocess an array to answer inclusive range-sum queries without updates.
hints: Can each query reuse totals computed once?
Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i values. Range [l,r] is prefix[r+1]-prefix[l].
303.approach: An extra leading zero makes ranges starting at index zero use the same formula.
303.cost: O(n) preprocessing time and space; O(1) per query. Use long[] if total sums can exceed int.

238.title: Product of Array Except Self
238.prompt: Return each position’s product of all other elements without division, in linear time.
hints: Combine information strictly to the left and strictly to the right.
Write prefix products into the answer, then multiply by a running suffix product.
238.approach: Before visiting index i in the backward pass, suffix contains exactly the product after i. Handles zeros without special division cases.
238.cost: O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space excluding the O(n) returned array. Products are assumed to fit int as in the problem constraints.

56.title: Merge Intervals
56.prompt: Merge all overlapping closed intervals. Touching endpoints count as overlap.
hints: Sorting can make intervals that need merging adjacent.
Sort by start, extend the current merged interval while next.start <= current.end.
56.approach: Once the next start exceeds the current end, no later interval can overlap the current one.
56.cost: O(n log n) time; O(n) space including output and object-array sorting workspace. The input array is reordered.

179.title: Largest Number
179.prompt: Arrange nonnegative integers to form the largest concatenated number.
hints: Ordinary numeric or lexicographic sorting does not resolve pairs such as 3 and 30.
Compare the concatenations a+b and b+a.
179.approach: Place a before b exactly when a+b is larger. An all-zero input must return a single zero.
179.cost: O(n log n · d) time for maximum digit length d; O(nd) space for strings/output plus sorting workspace.

704.title: Binary Search
704.prompt: Find target in an ascending array of distinct values, or return -1.
hints: A comparison can eliminate half the candidates.
Maintain a closed candidate interval [left,right]; discard mid after checking it.
704.approach: If present, target remains in the candidate interval after every update.
704.cost: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space. Each comparison halves the remaining candidate interval.

34.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
34.prompt: Return the first and last indices of target in a sorted array, or [-1,-1].
hints: A normal search finds any occurrence, not necessarily a boundary.
Find the first index >= target and the first index > target using separate lower-bound searches.
34.approach: The target occupies a contiguous block between the two boundaries. The end may equal n.
34.cost: O(log n) time for two searches; O(1) space. Using a strict flag avoids target+1 overflow.

33.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
33.prompt: Find target in a rotated ascending array with distinct values.
hints: At least one half is still sorted.
Identify the sorted half, then test whether target lies within its value range.
33.approach: Discard a half only after proving target cannot occur there; distinctness makes the sorted-half test unambiguous.
33.cost: O(log n) time and O(1) space under the distinct-values constraint. Duplicates require additional handling and can lead to O(n).

875.title: Koko Eating Bananas
875.prompt: Find the smallest integer eating speed that finishes all positive piles within h hours; h is at least the number of piles.
hints: If a speed works, do all larger speeds work?
Binary-search speed from 1 to the largest pile; sum ceil(pile/speed) to test feasibility.
875.approach: Feasibility is false then true. Keep a known-feasible upper boundary and locate the first feasible speed.
875.cost: O(n log M) time, where M is the largest pile; O(1) extra space. Each candidate speed requires an O(n) scan.

1011.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
1011.prompt: Find minimum ship capacity to transport positive weights in order within days days.
hints: A capacity can be checked greedily without finding the optimal capacity first.
Search between max(weight) and sum(weights); count days used by filling each day in order.
1011.approach: For fixed capacity, taking the longest fitting prefix each day minimizes the number of days. Feasibility is monotone.
1011.cost: O(n log S) time, S=sum(weights); O(1) space. int sums are safe under the stated LeetCode constraints; use long for larger totals.

410.title: Split Array Largest Sum
410.prompt: Split nonnegative values into exactly k nonempty contiguous groups, minimizing the largest group sum.
hints: A bound on the largest group sum defines a yes/no question.
Greedily count groups needed under a bound; search from max value to total sum.
410.approach: If at most k groups suffice, nonnegative groups can be split further to reach exactly k without increasing their sums.
410.cost: O(n log(S+1)) time for total S; O(1) space. The nonnegative constraint is essential.

57.title: Insert Interval
57.prompt: Insert one closed interval into sorted, disjoint closed intervals and merge overlaps.
hints: The existing order lets you avoid sorting again.
Copy intervals strictly before the new one, absorb overlaps, then copy the suffix.
57.approach: Each interval belongs to exactly one of three phases: before, overlapping, after.
57.cost: O(n) time and O(n) output/reference-list space. Unchanged intervals are shared with the input rather than copied.

435.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
435.prompt: Remove the fewest intervals so the rest do not overlap. Touching endpoints are allowed.
hints: Equivalently, keep the largest compatible subset.
Sort by end and keep each interval whose start is at least the previous kept end.
435.approach: The earliest-ending choice leaves at least as much room as any competing first choice; repeat this exchange argument.
435.cost: O(n log n) time; O(n) Java object-array sorting workspace. The subsequent greedy scan uses O(1) auxiliary state.

1094.title: Car Pooling
1094.prompt: Trips give passenger count, pickup, and drop-off positions. Determine whether capacity is ever exceeded; drop-off frees capacity at that position.
hints: Only pickup and drop-off positions change the number onboard.
Add passengers at start and subtract at end in a sorted event map; accumulate deltas.
1094.approach: Combine all deltas at the same position before checking capacity, matching drop-off/pickup sharing.
1094.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for up to 2n distinct events. A bounded-coordinate difference array is another option.

2406.title: Divide Intervals Into Minimum Number of Groups
2406.prompt: Assign closed intervals to the fewest groups so intervals within a group do not intersect.
hints: The answer is the maximum number of simultaneously active intervals.
For integer endpoints, add +1 at start and -1 at end+1, then take the maximum prefix total.
2406.approach: Closed endpoints stay active through end. Using end+1 implements that rule directly.
2406.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) space. long event coordinates avoid end+1 overflow.

1109.title: Corporate Flight Bookings
1109.prompt: Each booking adds seats to an inclusive range of numbered flights. Return the total seats for every flight.
hints: Many range additions can be recorded by their boundary changes.
Add at first-1, subtract at last when it is inside the array, then take a prefix sum.
1109.approach: Each booking contributes from its start until its cancellation event just after its final flight.
1109.cost: O(b+n) time for b bookings and n flights; O(n) returned array, O(1) extra state beyond it.

206.title: Reverse Linked List
206.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
hints: Changing a next pointer can lose access to the remaining list.
Save next, reverse the current link, then advance prev and current.
206.approach: prev is the reversed processed prefix; current starts the untouched suffix.
206.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Nodes are relinked in place.

21.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
21.prompt: Merge two sorted linked lists by relinking their nodes.
hints: A dummy head removes the special case of choosing the first output node.
Repeatedly append the smaller head, then attach the remaining suffix.
21.approach: The output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest processed nodes.
21.cost: O(m+n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Reuses input nodes; does not allocate an output copy.

19.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
19.prompt: Remove the nth node from the end; n is valid.
hints: A fixed distance between two pointers can convert an end-relative position to one pass.
Start both at a dummy node, advance fast n times, then move both until fast.next is null.
19.approach: slow ends immediately before the node to remove, including when that node is the head.
19.cost: O(L) time for list length L, O(1) extra space. The two passes of pointer movement together are still linear.

141.title: Linked List Cycle
141.prompt: Determine whether following next pointers eventually repeats a node.
hints: Two runners at different speeds behave differently on a path and a cycle.
Move slow one step and fast two. Compare node identities after moving.
141.approach: In a cycle the relative distance advances by one per iteration modulo cycle length, so the pointers meet.
141.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space, where n counts distinct reachable nodes. An acyclic list terminates; a cyclic one meets within prefix length plus cycle length iterations.

876.title: Middle of the Linked List
876.prompt: Return the middle node; for even length return the second middle.
hints: How far has a one-step pointer traveled when a two-step pointer reaches the end?
Move slow once and fast twice while fast and fast.next exist.
876.approach: After t iterations, slow is at index t and fast has advanced 2t steps.

287.title: Find the Duplicate Number
287.prompt: An array of n+1 numbers contains values in [1,n] and exactly one duplicated value, possibly repeated more than twice. Find it without modifying the array and with constant extra space.
hints: Interpret each value as the index of the next node.
Run Floyd’s meeting phase from index 0, then reset one pointer to 0 and move both one step.
287.approach: The functional graph reachable from index 0 has a cycle. Its entry is the duplicate because it has multiple incoming references.
287.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. The graph interpretation requires the value range [1,n].

20.title: Valid Parentheses
20.prompt: Check proper matching and nesting of (), [], and {}.
hints: The most recent unmatched opener must close first.
Push the expected closing bracket; compare each closer with the stack top.
20.approach: The stack records all outstanding closing obligations in reverse order.
20.cost: O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space for unmatched openers. The input is assumed to contain only the six bracket characters.

150.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
150.prompt: Evaluate a valid postfix arithmetic expression; division truncates toward zero.
hints: An operator consumes the two most recent unfinished results.
Pop right operand first, then left. Push the computed result.
150.approach: Each stack entry is the result of a completed subexpression waiting to be combined.
150.cost: O(n) time for n bounded-length tokens; O(n) stack space. With arbitrary-length tokens include total token length in parsing cost.

155.title: Min Stack
155.prompt: Support push, pop, top, and getMin in constant time per operation.
hints: Store enough history to restore the minimum after a pop.
With each pushed value, save the minimum of all values up to that stack entry.
155.approach: Every entry contains the correct minimum for the stack prefix ending at that entry.
155.cost: O(1) amortized push/pop with ArrayDeque; O(1) top/getMin. O(n) storage. Operations other than push are called only on a nonempty stack.
155.example: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin() → -3; pop(), getMin() → -2

739.title: Daily Temperatures
739.prompt: For each day, return the number of days until a strictly warmer temperature, or zero.
hints: Some earlier days remain unresolved until a warmer day appears.
Keep unresolved indices in nonincreasing temperature order; pop while current temperature is greater.
739.approach: A popped day sees its first warmer day now, because all intervening days failed to pop it.
739.cost: O(n) time: each index is pushed once and popped at most once. O(n) auxiliary stack, plus O(n) output.

496.title: Next Greater Element I
496.prompt: For each value in nums1, find the first greater value to its right in nums2; nums1 is a subset and nums2 has distinct values.
hints: Solve the next-greater question for nums2 once.
Maintain a decreasing stack of values, recording a mapping when a larger value pops them.
496.approach: Distinct values let the mapping use values directly; duplicates would generally require indices.
496.cost: Expected O(m+n) time and O(n) auxiliary space, for lengths m and n.

84.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
84.prompt: Find the largest rectangular area under unit-width histogram bars.
hints: A bar’s full usable width becomes known when a smaller bar arrives.
Use increasing-height indices; on a pop, the new top is the previous smaller boundary and i is the right boundary.
84.approach: A sentinel zero flushes remaining bars. Equal heights may remain together; at least one receives the full width.
84.cost: O(n) time and O(n) stack space. Each index enters and leaves once; area fits int under the original constraints.

239.title: Sliding Window Maximum
239.prompt: Return the maximum for every contiguous window of size k, with 1 <= k <= n.
hints: A later, larger value makes an earlier, smaller value useless for future maxima.
Store indices in decreasing value order; remove expired indices from front and dominated ones from back.
239.approach: The deque front is the largest unexpired candidate. A dominated index expires earlier and cannot beat its dominator.
239.cost: O(n) time; O(k) auxiliary space plus O(n-k+1) output. Each index is inserted and removed at most once.

1438.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
1438.prompt: Find the longest contiguous subarray whose maximum minus minimum is at most limit.
hints: Checking every pair is equivalent to checking maximum minus minimum.
Use one decreasing deque for maxima and one increasing deque for minima; shrink until valid.
1438.approach: Both fronts describe the current window’s extrema; expanding cannot reduce the range, so shrinking is safe.
1438.cost: O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space. Each index enters and leaves each deque once.

862.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
862.prompt: Find the shortest nonempty subarray with sum at least k, allowing negative numbers, or return -1.
hints: Prefix sums convert the target to a difference; some previous prefixes are dominated.
Keep increasing prefix sums in a deque. Pop front when it forms a valid range; pop back when current prefix is no larger.
862.approach: A later prefix with a smaller/equal sum is always a better future start. A front that already forms a valid range cannot improve its length at a later end.
862.cost: O(n) time and O(n) space for prefix sums and deque. Every prefix index enters and exits at most once.

104.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
104.prompt: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
hints: What answer can each child return to its parent?
The depth of null is 0; any node has depth 1 + max(left depth,right depth).
104.approach: Induction on subtrees: correct child depths give the correct maximum path through the parent.
104.cost: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space for tree height h: O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
104.example: root 3 with children 9 and 20; 20 has children 15 and 7 → 3

543.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
543.prompt: Return the longest path length in edges between any two nodes.
hints: A longest path can turn at a node and use both child subtrees.
Return height upward; separately maximize leftHeight+rightHeight.
543.approach: Returning the whole diameter upward would be wrong: a parent can extend only one descending branch.
543.cost: O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space. Resetting the field makes repeated calls safe.
543.example: Tree [1,2,3,4,5] in level order → diameter 3 edges

236.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
236.prompt: Find the lowest common ancestor of two distinct node objects p and q, both present in the tree.
hints: Each subtree can report whether it contains a target or their ancestor.
Return the node when it is p or q. If both recursive sides return nonnull, current is the answer.
236.approach: If targets split across the two child subtrees, current is their lowest shared ancestor; otherwise propagate the nonnull result.
236.cost: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space. If nodes may be absent, add explicit presence validation.

102.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
102.prompt: Return node values grouped by depth from the root.
hints: A queue visits nodes in increasing distance from the root.
Capture the queue size before processing each level.
102.approach: At the beginning of a level, the queue contains exactly that level’s nodes.
102.cost: O(n) time; O(w) auxiliary queue space for maximum width w, plus O(n) output.

199.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
199.prompt: Return the visible value at each depth when viewed from the right.
hints: Which node is last if a level is processed from left to right?
Use BFS and record the last node of each captured level size.
199.approach: Enqueuing left before right preserves left-to-right order within every level.
199.cost: O(n) time, O(w) auxiliary queue space, and O(h) output.

111.title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
111.prompt: Return the number of nodes on the shortest root-to-leaf path.
hints: A missing child is not a leaf path.
Use BFS; return as soon as a node has both children null.
111.approach: BFS processes increasing depths, so the first actual leaf gives the shortest root-to-leaf path.
111.cost: O(n) worst-case time and O(w) queue space. Early exit may visit fewer nodes.

98.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
98.prompt: Determine whether every node obeys strict BST ordering, with all left descendants smaller and all right descendants larger.
hints: Checking only immediate children misses ancestor constraints.
Carry exclusive lower and upper bounds into each subtree.
98.approach: Every descendant must satisfy all ancestor restrictions; the propagated interval captures their intersection.
98.cost: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space. long bounds allow Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE as legal node values.

230.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
230.prompt: Return the kth smallest value in a BST, with valid k.
hints: Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted.
Simulate inorder with a stack; decrement k when visiting each popped node.
230.approach: All nodes in the left subtree are visited before the node and its right subtree.
230.cost: O(h+k) time and O(h) stack space, worst-case O(n) time.

235.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
235.prompt: Find the lowest common ancestor of two existing nodes in a strict BST.
hints: BST ordering tells you whether both targets lie on the same side.
Move left if both values are smaller, right if both are larger; otherwise return current.
235.approach: The first split point, including a target itself, is the lowest node that can contain both targets.
235.cost: O(h) time and O(1) extra space; O(log n) time only if the tree is balanced.

200.title: Number of Islands
200.prompt: Count four-directionally connected components of land in a rectangular grid.
hints: One search can mark an entire island.
On each unvisited land cell, increment the count and flood-fill its component.
200.approach: Every island causes exactly one new search; marking on entry prevents revisiting. This implementation mutates the grid.
200.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case recursion space. A long island can overflow Java’s call stack; use an explicit stack/queue for large grids.

994.title: Rotting Oranges
994.prompt: Every minute, rotten oranges infect fresh four-directional neighbors. Return minutes to rot all fresh oranges, or -1.
hints: All initially rotten cells act as simultaneous distance-zero sources.
Enqueue all rotten cells first, then process BFS layers while tracking the remaining fresh count.
994.approach: A fresh cell is marked rotten when enqueued, so it is scheduled once at its earliest infection minute.
994.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) queue space; mutates the grid.

207.title: Course Schedule
207.prompt: Determine whether all courses can be completed given prerequisite pairs [course, prerequisite].
hints: A course with no remaining prerequisites can be completed now.
Build edges prerequisite→course, enqueue indegree-zero nodes, and remove their outgoing dependencies.
207.approach: If fewer than all vertices are processed, the remaining directed graph contains a cycle.
207.cost: O(V+E) time and space including adjacency lists, indegrees, and queue. Each vertex is processed once and each edge removed once.

210.title: Course Schedule II
210.prompt: Return a valid ordering of all courses, or an empty array if impossible.
hints: Extend dependency elimination by recording the order.
Append each popped indegree-zero node to the result; verify that all nodes were popped.
210.approach: Every course enters the output only after all its prerequisites, so a complete output is a valid topological ordering.
210.cost: O(V+E) time and space, including the graph and output. Multiple correct orders may exist.

802.title: Find Eventual Safe States
802.prompt: Return nodes from which every possible directed path eventually terminates.
hints: Reverse the question: which nodes lead only to already-safe nodes?
Reverse edges, initialize original terminal nodes, and repeatedly reduce predecessors’ remaining outgoing counts.
802.approach: A node becomes safe only after all its outgoing edges lead to safe nodes. Nodes on or leading into cycles remain.
802.cost: O(V+E) time and space. Scanning node indices at the end produces sorted output without sorting.

684.title: Redundant Connection
684.prompt: An undirected tree has one extra edge. Return the removable edge appearing last in input order.
hints: An edge creates a cycle when its endpoints are already connected.
Process edges with union-find. A failed union identifies the cycle-closing edge.
684.approach: Before an edge is processed, DSU represents connectivity using earlier edges; joining vertices already connected creates a cycle.
684.cost: O(n α(n)) amortized time and O(n) space with union by size and path compression; α is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively tiny for practical n.

547.title: Number of Provinces
547.prompt: Count connected components in an undirected adjacency matrix.
hints: Every successful union reduces the number of components by one.
Initialize n components and union each connected upper-triangle pair.
547.approach: DSU partitions vertices into exactly the components induced by the processed edges.
547.cost: O(n² α(n)) upper-bound time, O(n) auxiliary space excluding the input matrix. Matrix scanning alone is O(n²); DFS is also a natural solution.

1319.title: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected
1319.prompt: You may relocate redundant undirected cables. Return the fewest relocations to connect all computers, or -1.
hints: Connecting n computers needs at least n-1 cables.
After checking cable count, count DSU components; the answer is components-1.
1319.approach: With enough total cables, cycles provide at least the spare cables needed to connect the remaining components.
1319.cost: O(n + E α(n)) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

743.title: Network Delay Time
743.prompt: Directed nonnegative weighted edges describe signal travel times. Return when all n nodes receive a signal from k, or -1.
hints: Fewest edges is different from smallest total weight.
Use a min-heap of tentative distances and relax outgoing edges; ignore stale heap entries.
743.approach: The smallest unsettled distance is final because nonnegative edges cannot create a cheaper route through a farther node.
743.cost: O(V + E log(E+1)) time and O(V+E) space with lazy duplicate heap entries. Under a simple graph this is commonly written O((V+E) log V). Return cast is safe under the original bounds.

1631.title: Path With Minimum Effort
1631.prompt: On a height grid, minimize the maximum absolute height difference along a four-directional path.
hints: Path cost is a bottleneck maximum rather than a sum.
Dijkstra still works with candidate=max(current effort, edge difference).
1631.approach: Extending a path cannot reduce its bottleneck, so the minimum-effort heap extraction is safe.
1631.cost: O(RC log(RC)) time and O(RC) space since the grid has O(RC) edges. Height differences fit int under problem bounds.

1514.title: Path with Maximum Probability
1514.prompt: Given undirected edges with independent success probabilities in [0,1], maximize the product along a path from start to end.
hints: Multiplying by a probability cannot improve an already smaller path above its current value.
Use a max-heap and relax products when they improve a node’s best probability.
1514.approach: The greatest tentative probability can be finalized because extending any other path cannot increase its product.
1514.cost: O(V+E log(E+1)) time and O(V+E) space for lazy heap entries and adjacency lists.

347.title: Top K Frequent Elements
347.prompt: Return the k most frequent values, in any order.
hints: Count first; retain only the k strongest candidates.
Use a min-heap keyed by frequency; whenever size exceeds k, remove the weakest.
347.approach: After each insertion, the heap holds the k most frequent values seen so far, or all values if fewer exist.
347.cost: Expected O(n + u log(k+1)) time for u unique values; O(u+k) auxiliary space plus O(k) output. A bucket approach can achieve expected O(n) time.

23.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
23.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
hints: Only the head of each remaining list can be the next global minimum.
Heap the nonnull heads; pop the smallest and insert its successor.
23.approach: The heap contains one frontier node per nonempty list, enough to identify the next output node.
23.cost: O(k + N log(k+1)) time for N total nodes, including scanning k list slots; O(k) heap space. Reuses existing nodes.

295.title: Find Median from Data Stream
295.prompt: Support adding integers and retrieving the median of all values seen.
hints: Split values into a lower half and upper half.
Keep a max-heap for the lower half and min-heap for the upper; lower has equal size or one extra.
295.approach: All lower values are <= all upper values. Balanced sizes make the middle element(s) available at the heap tops.
295.cost: O(log n) per insertion, O(1) per median query, O(n) storage. Query assumes at least one inserted value.

78.title: Subsets
78.prompt: Return all subsets of an array of distinct integers.
hints: Every partial selection is already a valid subset.
Add a copy of the current path, then choose each remaining index and recurse from the following index.
78.approach: Increasing indices give each subset exactly one construction path. Copying prevents later backtracking from changing saved answers.
78.cost: O(n·2^n) time including copying, O(n) auxiliary recursion/path space, O(n·2^n) output.

46.title: Permutations
46.prompt: Return all orderings of distinct integers.
hints: Unlike combinations, every position can choose any unused value.
Track used indices, choose one, recurse, then undo both the path and used flag.
46.approach: Each path chooses each value once; different ordered choices create different permutations.
46.cost: O(n·n!) time including copying and candidate scans, O(n) auxiliary space, O(n·n!) output.

39.title: Combination Sum
39.prompt: Return unique combinations of distinct positive candidate values totaling target; values may be reused.
hints: Combinations ignore order, but repetition is allowed.
Use a start index and recurse with i rather than i+1 when choosing candidate i again.
39.approach: Nondecreasing choice indices prevent reordered duplicates; positive candidates ensure the remaining target decreases.
39.cost: Let c be candidate count and d=floor(target/min candidate). A loose upper bound is O((c+1)^(d+1) + z·d) time, including z output copies; O(d) auxiliary space and O(z·d) output. Actual work depends strongly on valid combinations.

70.title: Climbing Stairs
70.prompt: Count ways to climb n stairs using steps of size one or two; n >= 1.
hints: Classify paths by their final step.
ways[i]=ways[i-1]+ways[i-2], with ways[0]=ways[1]=1.
70.approach: The final step partitions all paths into two disjoint groups; keeping the previous two totals is sufficient.
70.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. int fits the problem’s n<=45 constraint; larger n requires a wider or arbitrary-precision type.

198.title: House Robber
198.prompt: Maximize the sum of nonnegative house values without choosing adjacent houses.
hints: At each house, decide whether to skip it or take it.
best[i]=max(best[i-1],best[i-2]+value[i]); retain two previous totals.
198.approach: Every valid optimum either skips the current house or includes it and therefore excludes the preceding house.
198.cost: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

139.title: Word Break
139.prompt: Determine whether a string can be segmented into dictionary words; words may be reused.
hints: Choosing the first matching word can block a later valid segmentation.
Let reachable[end] mean s[0:end] is segmentable. Try every earlier reachable split point within the longest word length.
139.approach: The final word of a valid segmentation starts at some reachable prefix boundary. Enumerating all boundaries avoids the greedy trap.
139.cost: Let n=string length, L=min(max word length,n), W=total dictionary characters, D=number of words. O(W+nL²) expected time with Java substring copying and hashing; O(n+D+L) peak auxiliary space, excluding input strings. The abstract O(nL) transition count alone omits string costs.

62.title: Unique Paths
62.prompt: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right of an m×n grid, moving only right or down.
hints: The final move arrives from above or left.
Use dp[r][c]=dp[r-1][c]+dp[r][c-1]; first row and column have one path.
62.approach: Each path has exactly one final predecessor, so adding their counts is exhaustive without double-counting.
62.cost: O(mn) time and O(mn) space. A rolling row reduces space to O(n). Answer fits int under the original problem guarantee.

64.title: Minimum Path Sum
64.prompt: Find the minimum sum along a right/down path through a nonnegative grid.
hints: Replace counting predecessor paths with choosing the cheaper predecessor.
Initialize the origin, treat first row/column separately, then add the cell cost to min(above,left).
64.approach: Every path to a cell ends at one of those two predecessors; optimal substructure justifies taking their minimum.
64.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) space without changing the input. Rolling-row DP reduces auxiliary space to O(C).

63.title: Unique Paths II
63.prompt: Count right/down paths through a grid with blocked cells marked 1.
hints: A blocked cell contributes zero paths, even at the start or end.
Use a rolling row; set blocked entries to zero and add the left count for open cells.
63.approach: Before updating a column, dp[c] is the above count; after updating c-1, dp[c-1] is the left count.
63.cost: O(RC) time and O(C) auxiliary space.

416.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
416.prompt: Determine whether positive integers can be split into two groups of equal sum, using every value once.
hints: One group must sum to half the total.
Reject an odd total. Use boolean reachable sums; scan sums downward for each number.
416.approach: Descending order ensures each number is used at most once because reachable[sum-value] still belongs to the previous item stage.
416.cost: O(nS) time and O(S) space for S=total/2. This is pseudo-polynomial: the numeric sum matters, not only the number of input bits.

322.title: Coin Change
322.prompt: With unlimited positive-denomination coins, return the minimum number to form amount, or -1.
hints: Choosing the largest coin first is not always optimal.
Let dp[a] be minimum coins for amount a; try every possible final coin.
322.approach: Each optimal combination has a final coin; removing it leaves an optimal solution for the remaining amount.
322.cost: O(cA) time for c coin denominations and amount A, O(A) auxiliary space.

518.title: Coin Change II
518.prompt: Count combinations of unlimited distinct positive-denomination coins that total amount; ordering does not matter.
hints: Counting combinations requires controlling when a coin type becomes available.
Loop coin types outside and amounts upward inside; start dp[0]=1.
518.approach: Each combination is counted when its largest processed coin type is added; upward iteration permits repeated use of that coin.
518.cost: O(cA) time and O(A) space. Swapping loop order would count ordered sequences instead.

1143.title: Longest Common Subsequence
1143.prompt: Return the longest subsequence length shared by two strings; characters need not be contiguous.
hints: Define the answer for a pair of prefixes.
If final characters match, take diagonal+1; otherwise take max(skip left character,skip right character).
1143.approach: Matching final characters can extend an optimal smaller pair; when they differ, at least one final character must be omitted.
1143.cost: O(mn) time and O(mn) space. A rolling row reduces memory if only length is required.

72.title: Edit Distance
72.prompt: Find the minimum insertions, deletions, and replacements to transform word1 into word2.
hints: Track how many edits convert one prefix to another.
Initialize empty-prefix costs; if characters differ take 1+min(delete,insert,replace).
72.approach: The final edit must be one of the three operations, each leaving a smaller prefix problem.
72.cost: O(mn) time and O(mn) space; O(min(m,n)) space is possible with a rolling row.

300.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
300.prompt: Return the length of a strictly increasing subsequence in an integer array.
hints: First define the best subsequence ending at each index.
For every j<i with nums[j]<nums[i], consider extending the best subsequence ending at j.
300.approach: Every nontrivial increasing subsequence ending at i has a previous endpoint j with a smaller value.
300.cost: O(n²) time and O(n) space for this DP. A tails array with lower-bound binary search improves time to O(n log n).

55.title: Jump Game
55.prompt: Each nonnegative value is the maximum jump length from that index. Can you reach the last index?
hints: You need reachable coverage, not a commitment to a particular jump.
Scan reachable indices and update the farthest reachable position.
55.approach: All indices up to farthest are reachable because jump lengths up to each maximum are allowed.
55.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Index arithmetic fits int for the original bounds.

121.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
121.prompt: Choose one earlier buy and later sell to maximize profit, or do nothing.
hints: For a sale today, which earlier purchase price is best?
Track the lowest price so far and the best profit using each price as a sale candidate.
121.approach: For every sale day, the smallest preceding price is the optimal buy; considering all sale days covers all transactions.
121.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Updating minimum first permits a zero-profit same-day comparison, which does not alter the optimal answer.

208.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
208.prompt: Implement insert, exact-word search, and prefix search for lowercase English words.
hints: Many words can share the same prefix path.
Each node has 26 child slots and a separate end-of-word marker.
208.approach: Reaching a node proves the prefix exists; exact search additionally requires its terminal marker.
208.cost: O(L) time per operation for length L; O(26T) storage for T trie nodes. toCharArray uses O(L) temporary space here; charAt loops could avoid that allocation.

211.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
211.prompt: Store lowercase words and search patterns where dot matches any one letter.
hints: An ordinary character follows one child, while a wildcard branches.
Use a trie plus DFS over all nonnull children when the pattern character is dot.
